claim: YAP and TAZ are transcriptional co-activators recruited to target sites by TEAD proteins.
source: The YAP and TAZ paralogs are transcriptional co-activators recruited to target sites by TEAD proteins.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as established background information.

claim: YAP and TAZ are recruited by JUNB and STAT3.
source: Here, we show that YAP and TAZ are also recruited by JUNB (a member of the AP-1 family) and STAT3, key transcription factors that mediate an epigenetic switch linking inflammation to cellular transformation.
evidence: This is the primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by multiple experiments throughout the manuscript.

claim: YAP and TAZ directly interact with JUNB and STAT3 via a WW domain important for transformation.
source: YAP and TAZ directly interact with JUNB and STAT3 via a WW domain important for transformation, and they stimulate transcriptional activation by AP-1 proteins.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation experiments with recombinant proteins and domain deletion studies shown in Figure 3.

claim: YAP and TAZ stimulate transcriptional activation by AP-1 proteins.
source: YAP and TAZ directly interact with JUNB and STAT3 via a WW domain important for transformation, and they stimulate transcriptional activation by AP-1 proteins.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 2C.

claim: JUNB, STAT3, and TEAD co-localize at virtually all YAP/TAZ target sites.
source: JUNB, STAT3, and TEAD co-localize at virtually all YAP/TAZ target sites, yet many target sites only contain individual AP-1, TEAD, or STAT3 motifs.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing overlapping binding profiles in Figure 5A and peak summit distance analysis in Figure 5B.

claim: Many YAP/TAZ target sites only contain individual AP-1, TEAD, or STAT3 motifs.
source: JUNB, STAT3, and TEAD co-localize at virtually all YAP/TAZ target sites, yet many target sites only contain individual AP-1, TEAD, or STAT3 motifs.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: YAP/TAZ is recruited by different forms of an AP-1/STAT3/TEAD complex depending on the recruiting motif.
source: This observation and differences in relative crosslinking efficiencies of JUNB, TEAD, and STAT3 at YAP/TAZ target sites suggest that YAP/TAZ is recruited by different forms of an AP-1/STAT3/TEAD complex depending on the recruiting motif.
evidence: Supported by differential crosslinking efficiencies shown in Figure 6F and the presence of individual motifs at target sites.

claim: Different classes of YAP/TAZ target sites are associated with largely non-overlapping genes with distinct functions.
source: The different classes of YAP/TAZ target sites are associated with largely non-overlapping genes with distinct functions.
evidence: Supported by gene overlap analysis in Figure 6G and GO analysis in Supplementary file 4.

claim: A small minority of target sites are YAP- or TAZ-specific.
source: A small minority of target sites are YAP- or TAZ-specific, and they are associated with different sequence motifs and gene classes from shared YAP/TAZ target sites.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis in knockout cell lines shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: YAP- and TAZ-specific sites are associated with different sequence motifs and gene classes from shared YAP/TAZ target sites.
source: A small minority of target sites are YAP- or TAZ-specific, and they are associated with different sequence motifs and gene classes from shared YAP/TAZ target sites.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and GO analysis in Supplementary file 2.

claim: Genes containing either the AP-1 or TEAD class of YAP/TAZ sites are associated with poor survival of breast cancer patients with the triple-negative form of the disease.
source: Genes containing either the AP-1 or TEAD class of YAP/TAZ sites are associated with poor survival of breast cancer patients with the triple-negative form of the disease.
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7D-E.

claim: YAP and TAZ are paralogous proteins with 63% sequence similarity.
source: Internal and external signals relayed through the Hippo pathway converge on YAP and TAZ, paralogous proteins with 63% sequence similarity that are the major effectors of this pathway (Piccolo et al., 2014; Totaro et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP and TAZ are the major effectors of the Hippo pathway.
source: Internal and external signals relayed through the Hippo pathway converge on YAP and TAZ, paralogous proteins with 63% sequence similarity that are the major effectors of this pathway (Piccolo et al., 2014; Totaro et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Once activated, YAP/TAZ translocate into nucleus and act as transcriptional co-activators.
source: Once activated, YAP/TAZ translocate into nucleus and act as transcriptional co-activators, most notably by interacting with the TEAD family of DNA-binding transcription factors (Piccolo et al., 2014; Totaro et al., 2018; Ma et al., 2019; Moya and Halder, 2019).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Deregulation of YAP/TAZ activity is frequently observed in various human cancers.
source: Deregulation of YAP/TAZ activity is frequently observed in various human cancers, contributing to cancer initiation, progression, and metastasis (Johnson and Halder, 2014; Yu et al., 2015; Zanconato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP/TAZ activation is linked to chemo-resistance in cancer therapy.
source: YAP/TAZ activation is also linked to chemo-resistance in cancer therapy (Johnson and Halder, 2014; Yu et al., 2015; Zanconato et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP and TAZ have distinct and overlapping cellular functions.
source: Genetic experiments indicate that YAP and TAZ have distinct and overlapping cellular functions (Plouffe et al., 2018; Shreberk-Shaked et al., 2020), but the molecular basis for the distinct functions is unknown.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The molecular basis for the distinct functions of YAP and TAZ is unknown.
source: Genetic experiments indicate that YAP and TAZ have distinct and overlapping cellular functions (Plouffe et al., 2018; Shreberk-Shaked et al., 2020), but the molecular basis for the distinct functions is unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the introduction.

claim: YAP/TAZ can synergize with JUN/FOS at composite regulatory elements containing both TEAD and AP-1 motifs.
source: Via its interaction with TEAD proteins, YAP/TAZ can synergize with JUN/FOS at composite regulatory elements containing both TEAD and AP-1 motifs (Zanconato et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP-TEAD signaling cooperates with AP-1 to promote basal cell carcinoma.
source: YAP-TEAD signaling cooperates with AP-1 to promote basal cell carcinoma (Maglic et al., 2018) and pancreatic cancer in mice (Park et al., 2020), and YAP/TAZ induces AP-1 transcription (Koo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP-TEAD signaling cooperates with AP-1 to promote pancreatic cancer in mice.
source: YAP-TEAD signaling cooperates with AP-1 to promote basal cell carcinoma (Maglic et al., 2018) and pancreatic cancer in mice (Park et al., 2020), and YAP/TAZ induces AP-1 transcription (Koo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP/TAZ induces AP-1 transcription.
source: YAP-TEAD signaling cooperates with AP-1 to promote basal cell carcinoma (Maglic et al., 2018) and pancreatic cancer in mice (Park et al., 2020), and YAP/TAZ induces AP-1 transcription (Koo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP can form a functional complex with β-catenin and TBX5 in cancer cells.
source: YAP can form a functional complex with β-catenin and TBX5 in cancer cells (Rosenbluh et al., 2012), YAP/TAZ can integrate into a SMAD–OCT4 complex in embryonic stem cells (Beyer et al., 2013), and a YAP-p73 complex plays a role in the DNA damage response (Beyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP/TAZ can integrate into a SMAD–OCT4 complex in embryonic stem cells.
source: YAP can form a functional complex with β-catenin and TBX5 in cancer cells (Rosenbluh et al., 2012), YAP/TAZ can integrate into a SMAD–OCT4 complex in embryonic stem cells (Beyer et al., 2013), and a YAP-p73 complex plays a role in the DNA damage response (Beyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: A YAP-p73 complex plays a role in the DNA damage response.
source: YAP can form a functional complex with β-catenin and TBX5 in cancer cells (Rosenbluh et al., 2012), YAP/TAZ can integrate into a SMAD–OCT4 complex in embryonic stem cells (Beyer et al., 2013), and a YAP-p73 complex plays a role in the DNA damage response (Beyer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP/TAZ directly interacts with the general co-activator BRD4 to increase RNA polymerase II recruitment and transcription of target genes.
source: In addition, YAP/TAZ directly interacts with the general co-activator BRD4 to increase RNA polymerase II recruitment and transcription of target genes (Zanconato et al., 2018), and YAP/TAZ activity is inhibited by a direct interaction with the SWI/SNF complex via the ARID1A subunit (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: YAP/TAZ activity is inhibited by a direct interaction with the SWI/SNF complex via the ARID1A subunit.
source: In addition, YAP/TAZ directly interacts with the general co-activator BRD4 to increase RNA polymerase II recruitment and transcription of target genes (Zanconato et al., 2018), and YAP/TAZ activity is inhibited by a direct interaction with the SWI/SNF complex via the ARID1A subunit (Chang et al., 2018).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: An epigenetic switch transforms breast cells via an inflammatory regulatory network controlled by the joint action of NF-κB, STAT3, and AP-1 transcription factors.
source: In previous work, we described an epigenetic switch that transforms breast cells via an inflammatory regulatory network controlled by the joint action of NF-κB, STAT3, and AP-1 transcription factors (Iliopoulos et al., 2009; Iliopoulos et al., 2010; Ji et al., 2018; Ji et al., 2019).
evidence: This is cited from the authors' previous work.

claim: Knockout of YAP or TAZ or both reduces growth under conditions of low attachment.
source: Knockout of YAP or TAZ or both (Figure 1A) reduces growth under conditions of low attachment (Figure 1B) and inhibits colony formation in soft agar (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Knockout of YAP or TAZ or both inhibits colony formation in soft agar.
source: Knockout of YAP or TAZ or both (Figure 1A) reduces growth under conditions of low attachment (Figure 1B) and inhibits colony formation in soft agar (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Knockout of YAP or TAZ has no effect on cell proliferation under standard conditions of high attachment.
source: In contrast, there is no effect on cell proliferation under standard conditions of high attachment (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of YAP or TAZ produces similar results to knockout.
source: Similar results are observed when YAP or TAZ expression is knocked down by siRNA (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: YAP and TAZ are important for cellular transformation in the ER-Src model.
source: Thus, YAP and TAZ are important for cellular transformation in this model.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the knockout and knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Depletion of YAP and/or TAZ strongly decreases STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705 during transformation.
source: Depletion of YAP and/or TAZ, but not JUNB, strongly decreases STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705 (STAT3-p, a marker of STAT3 activation) during transformation (Figure 2A), but it does not affect overall levels of STAT3 protein (Figure 2A) or mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depletion of YAP and/or TAZ does not affect overall levels of STAT3 protein.
source: Depletion of YAP and/or TAZ, but not JUNB, strongly decreases STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705 (STAT3-p, a marker of STAT3 activation) during transformation (Figure 2A), but it does not affect overall levels of STAT3 protein (Figure 2A) or mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Depletion of YAP and/or TAZ does not affect STAT3 mRNA levels.
source: Depletion of YAP and/or TAZ, but not JUNB, strongly decreases STAT3 phosphorylation at Tyr705 (STAT3-p, a marker of STAT3 activation) during transformation (Figure 2A), but it does not affect overall levels of STAT3 protein (Figure 2A) or mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: YAP and TAZ are important for induction of IL-6 transcription and secretion during transformation.
source: Consistent with this observation, YAP and TAZ are important for induction of IL-6 transcription and secretion during transformation (Figure 2B).
evidence: Supported by qPCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Depletion of YAP or TAZ inhibits transcriptional activation mediated by AP-1 factors.
source: In addition, depletion of YAP or TAZ (also STAT3 and JUNB) inhibits transcriptional activation mediated by AP-1 factors (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: YAP or TAZ depletion causes a slight increase in NF-κB activation.
source: In contrast, YAP or TAZ depletion causes a slight increase in NF-κB activation (Figure 2D), perhaps reflecting competition between the Hippo and NF-κB signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: YAP and TAZ protein levels in the nucleus are similar in the presence or absence of tamoxifen.
source: The effects of YAP and TAZ on AP-1 and STAT3 activity during transformation are not due to changes in YAP or TAZ protein levels in the nucleus, which are similar in the presence of absence of tamoxifen (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: YAP and TAZ each co-IP with STAT3 and JUNB in the nucleoplasm and chromatin fractions.
source: In the nucleoplasm and chromatin (but not cytoplasm) fractions, YAP and TAZ each co-IP with STAT3 and JUNB (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Co-IP of YAP/TAZ with STAT3 and JUNB is more efficient in transformed cells.
source: In general, co-IP is more efficient in transformed cells.
evidence: This is stated based on the co-IP results shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Direct pairwise YAP-STAT3, TAZ-STAT3, YAP-JUNB, and TAZ-JUNB interactions occur with recombinant proteins.
source: We confirmed direct pairwise YAP-STAT3, TAZ-STAT3, YAP-JUNB, and TAZ-JUNB interactions by performing co-IP experiments using histidine-tagged recombinant proteins generated in Escherichia coli (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with recombinant proteins shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The WW1 domain of YAP is critical for the interaction with STAT3 and JUNB.
source: The WW1 domain of YAP is critical for the interaction with STAT3 and JUNB, whereas removal of the YAP WW2 domain has no effect on these interactions.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with YAP deletion mutants shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Removal of the YAP WW2 domain has no effect on interactions with STAT3 and JUNB.
source: The WW1 domain of YAP is critical for the interaction with STAT3 and JUNB, whereas removal of the YAP WW2 domain has no effect on these interactions.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with YAP deletion mutants shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Deletion of the TAZ WW domain reduces, but does not eliminate, the interaction with either JUNB or STAT3.
source: Deletion of the TAZ WW domain reduces, but does not eliminate, the interaction with either JUNB or STAT3.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments with TAZ deletion mutants shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Removal of any WW domain has no effect on the interaction with the TEAD proteins.
source: Removal of any WW domain has no effect on the interaction with the TEAD proteins, whereas removal of the TEAD domain abolishes the interaction with the TEAD proteins.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Removal of the TEAD domain abolishes the interaction with the TEAD proteins.
source: Removal of any WW domain has no effect on the interaction with the TEAD proteins, whereas removal of the TEAD domain abolishes the interaction with the TEAD proteins.
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The TEAD domains of both YAP and TAZ are critical for the interaction with JUNB.
source: In addition, the TEAD domains of both YAP and TAZ are critical for the interaction with JUNB, but they contribute only partially to the interaction with STAT3 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The TEAD domains of YAP and TAZ contribute only partially to the interaction with STAT3.
source: In addition, the TEAD domains of both YAP and TAZ are critical for the interaction with JUNB, but they contribute only partially to the interaction with STAT3 (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by co-IP experiments shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Wild-type YAP or TAZ increase the level of transformation when overexpressed in parental MCF-10A cells.
source: When overexpressed in parental MCF-10A cells (i.e., lacking the ER-Src protein), wild-type YAP or TAZ increase the level of transformation, whereas derivatives lacking YAP-WW1 or TAZ-WW do not (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by low attachment growth assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: YAP derivatives lacking WW1 or TAZ derivatives lacking WW do not increase transformation when overexpressed.
source: When overexpressed in parental MCF-10A cells (i.e., lacking the ER-Src protein), wild-type YAP or TAZ increase the level of transformation, whereas derivatives lacking YAP-WW1 or TAZ-WW do not (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by low attachment growth assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Wild-type YAP, TAZ, and their WW deletion derivatives have no significant effect on cell proliferation under conditions of high attachment.
source: Like the wild-type proteins, none of these derivatives have a significant effect on cell proliferation under conditions of high attachment (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by high attachment growth assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The WW1 domain in YAP and the WW domain in TAZ are important for transformation.
source: Thus, the WW1 domain in YAP and the WW domain in TAZ, which are critical for interaction with JUNB and STAT3 but not TEAD proteins, are important for transformation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the domain deletion and transformation assay experiments.

claim: YAP and TAZ interactions with TEAD proteins are not sufficient for transformation.
source: These observations also indicate that YAP and TAZ interactions with TEAD proteins are not sufficient for transformation.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that WW domain deletions that do not affect TEAD interactions still abolish transformation.

claim: YAP and TAZ have very similar binding profiles in both the transformed and non-transformed states.
source: As expected from their being paralogs, YAP and TAZ have very similar binding profiles in both the transformed and non-transformed states (Figure 4A; overall Pearson correlation coefficient ~0.7).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The overall Pearson correlation coefficient between YAP and TAZ binding is approximately 0.7.
source: As expected from their being paralogs, YAP and TAZ have very similar binding profiles in both the transformed and non-transformed states (Figure 4A; overall Pearson correlation coefficient ~0.7).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Approximately 575 target sites (~2% of YAP/TAZ sites) appear specific for either YAP or TAZ.
source: Although nearly all target sites are bound by both YAP and TAZ, ~ 575 target sites (~2% of YAP/TAZ sites) appear specific for either YAP or TAZ (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Approximately 450 TAZ-specific sites and approximately 125 YAP-specific sites were confirmed by ChIP-seq in knockout cell lines.
source: In this manner, we confirmed ~450 TAZ-specific sites and ~125 YAP-specific sites (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq experiments in knockout cell lines shown in Figure 4B-C.

claim: More than 80% of YAP- and TAZ-specific sites are located within 150 base pairs upstream of a GENCODE-annotated transcription start site.
source: First, >80% of YAP- and TAZ-specific sites are located within 150 base pairs upstream of a GENCODE-annotated transcription start site (TSS), but <25% of shared YAP/TAZ sites are so localized (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by genomic location analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Less than 25% of shared YAP/TAZ sites are located within 150 base pairs upstream of a transcription start site.
source: First, >80% of YAP- and TAZ-specific sites are located within 150 base pairs upstream of a GENCODE-annotated transcription start site (TSS), but <25% of shared YAP/TAZ sites are so localized (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by genomic location analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: YAP- and TAZ-specific sites are much less likely to be located within JUNB and TEAD target regions compared to shared YAP/TAZ target sites.
source: Second, compared to shared YAP/TAZ target sites, YAP- and TAZ-specific sites are much less likely to be located within JUNB and TEAD target regions (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by overlap analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: TAZ-specific peaks are enriched in unique motifs.
source: Fourth, the TAZ-specific peaks are enriched in unique motifs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and see below).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: YAP/TAZ, TEAD, STAT3, and JUNB have very similar binding profiles.
source: Consistent with previous results for YAP/TAZ/TEAD/AP-1 (Zanconato et al., 2015) and AP-1/STAT3 (Ji et al., 2019), YAP/TAZ, TEAD, STAT3, and JUNB have very similar binding profiles.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq heatmap analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The median distances between YAP and TAZ peak summits are 25 bp.
source: YAP and TAZ peak summits are separated by 25 bp, indicating that these two proteins occupy the same sequences, although not necessarily at the same time.
evidence: Supported by peak summit distance analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The median distances between pairwise combinations of YAP, TAZ, JUNB, STAT3, and TEAD range between 31 and 44 bps.
source: Interestingly, the median distances between pairwise combinations of YAP, TAZ, JUNB, STAT3, and TEAD range between 31 and 44 bps (Figure 5B), indicating that the binding locations of these proteins are very close to each other and likely coincide.
evidence: Supported by peak summit distance analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Sequential ChIP in either order yields increased fold-enrichments of YAP with JUNB or STAT3 at the IL-6 enhancer.
source: At the IL-6 enhancer, sequential ChIP in either order yields increased fold-enrichments of YAP (Figure 5C) or TAZ (Figure 5D) with JUNB or STAT3 in non-transformed and transformed cells; similar results are observed at the SNX24 locus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequential ChIP data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Sequential ChIP in either order yields increased fold-enrichments of TAZ with JUNB or STAT3 at the IL-6 enhancer.
source: At the IL-6 enhancer, sequential ChIP in either order yields increased fold-enrichments of YAP (Figure 5C) or TAZ (Figure 5D) with JUNB or STAT3 in non-transformed and transformed cells; similar results are observed at the SNX24 locus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by sequential ChIP data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Sequential ChIP of JUNB and either YAP or TAZ on a transfected plasmid-borne locus containing six AP-1 motif sites shows increased fold-enrichment in transformed cells.
source: In addition, sequential ChIP (in both orders) of JUNB and either YAP or TAZ on a transfected plasmid-borne locus containing six AP-1 motif sites shows increased fold-enrichment in transformed cells, while this does not occur on a control plasmid locus lacking the AP-1 sites (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by sequential ChIP data on plasmid shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Approximately 30% of YAP/TAZ binding loci contain TEAD motifs.
source: As expected from YAP/TAZ being a co-activator of TEAD proteins, ~30% of YAP/TAZ binding loci contain TEAD motifs (Figure 6A), and the TEAD motif is the most significantly enriched motif within YAP/TAZ sites (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The TEAD motif is the most significantly enriched motif within YAP/TAZ sites.
source: As expected from YAP/TAZ being a co-activator of TEAD proteins, ~30% of YAP/TAZ binding loci contain TEAD motifs (Figure 6A), and the TEAD motif is the most significantly enriched motif within YAP/TAZ sites (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: A comparable number of YAP/TAZ target sites contain AP-1 motifs as contain TEAD motifs.
source: Interestingly, and in accordance with the direct interaction of JUNB and YAP/TAZ, a comparable number of YAP/TAZ target sites contain AP-1 motifs (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: YAP/TAZ target sites contain STAT3 motifs at 13% frequency.
source: YAP/TAZ target sites also contain STAT3 motifs, albeit at much lower frequency (13%) and minimal enrichment over control loci.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: All the TEAD, AP-1, and STAT3 motifs are centered around YAP/TAZ peak summits.
source: Importantly, all the TEAD, AP-1, and STAT3 motifs are centered around YAP/TAZ peak summits (Figure 6C), as expected for direct recruitment of YAP/TAZ by these DNA-binding transcription factors.
evidence: Supported by motif location histogram shown in Figure 6C.

claim: NF-κB motifs are not enriched or centered at YAP/TAZ target sites.
source: In contrast and as a negative control, NF-κB motifs are not enriched or centered at YAP/TAZ target sites (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: AP-1, TEAD, and STAT3 classes of YAP/TAZ sites exist with high FIMO scores for the defining motif and low scores for the other two motifs.
source: Of particular interest, we identified AP-1, TEAD, and (to a lesser extent) STAT3 classes of YAP/TAZ sites with high FIMO scores for the defining motif and low scores for the other two motifs (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by motif score analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Some YAP/TAZ target sites contain multiple motifs.
source: In accordance with previous observations (Zanconato et al., 2015), some YAP/TAZ target sites contain multiple motifs (Figure 6D).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Composite motifs occur at a higher frequency than expected by chance.
source: Such composite motifs occur at a higher frequency than expected by chance (Figure 6E), but composite AP-1/TEAD motifs (Zanconato et al., 2015) only make up 9% of the YAP/TAZ target sites, and thus are not required for YAP/TAZ recruitment.
evidence: Supported by motif co-occurrence analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Composite AP-1/TEAD motifs only make up 9% of the YAP/TAZ target sites.
source: Such composite motifs occur at a higher frequency than expected by chance (Figure 6E), but composite AP-1/TEAD motifs (Zanconato et al., 2015) only make up 9% of the YAP/TAZ target sites, and thus are not required for YAP/TAZ recruitment.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The JUNB:TEAD crosslinking ratio is strongly correlated with the quality of the AP-1 motif.
source: Strikingly, the JUNB:TEAD crosslinking ratio is strongly correlated with the quality of the AP-1 motif, whereas it is negatively correlated with the quality of the TEAD motif (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The JUNB:TEAD crosslinking ratio is negatively correlated with the quality of the TEAD motif.
source: Strikingly, the JUNB:TEAD crosslinking ratio is strongly correlated with the quality of the AP-1 motif, whereas it is negatively correlated with the quality of the TEAD motif (Figure 6F).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The motif recognized by the CEBP family of transcription factors occurs in 20% of YAP/TAZ sites.
source: Unexpectedly, the motif recognized by the CEBP family of transcription factors occurs in 20% of YAP/TAZ sites with an enrichment over control sites that is second-most behind that of TEAD motifs (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6A-B.

claim: CEBP motifs occur very close to YAP/TAZ peak summits.
source: CEBP motifs also occur very close to YAP/TAZ peak summits (Figure 6C), suggesting that one or more CEBP proteins can recruit YAP/TAZ to target sites.
evidence: Supported by motif location histogram shown in Figure 6C.

claim: CEBP motifs are strongly enriched within TEAD binding regions.
source: In addition, CEBP motifs are strongly enriched within TEAD binding regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and CEBP and TEAD motifs co-occur at YAP/TAZ sites at more than five times the rate that they co-occur in control regions (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: CEBP and TEAD motifs co-occur at YAP/TAZ sites at more than five times the rate that they co-occur in control regions.
source: In addition, CEBP motifs are strongly enriched within TEAD binding regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), and CEBP and TEAD motifs co-occur at YAP/TAZ sites at more than five times the rate that they co-occur in control regions (Figure 6E).
evidence: Supported by motif co-occurrence analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: 18% of YAP/TAZ binding sites lack AP-1, STAT3, TEAD, or CEBP motifs.
source: Lastly, a significant minority (18%) of YAP/TAZ binding sites lack AP-1, STAT3, TEAD, or CEBP motifs (Figure 6A), suggesting that other DNA-binding proteins can also recruit these co-activators.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Motifs for ETS family proteins are strongly enriched at TAZ-specific sites.
source: Instead, motifs for ETS family proteins are strongly enriched and the AP-1 motif is significantly depleted at TAZ-specific sites compared to control sites.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The AP-1 motif is significantly depleted at TAZ-specific sites compared to control sites.
source: Instead, motifs for ETS family proteins are strongly enriched and the AP-1 motif is significantly depleted at TAZ-specific sites compared to control sites.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Binding profiles for YAP, TAZ, STAT3, JUNB, and TEAD are extremely similar in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: As is the case in ER-Src cells, binding profiles for YAP, TAZ, STAT3, JUNB, and TEAD are extremely similar (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), and there are a small number of YAP- and TAZ-specific sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq heatmap analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The percentage of YAP/TAZ binding sites associated with AP-1, TEAD, and STAT3 motifs are comparable in ER-Src and MDA-MB-231 cell lines.
source: The percentage of YAP/TAZ binding sites associated with AP-1, TEAD, and STAT3 motifs are comparable in both cell lines (compare Figure 6A with Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B), and nearly half of the YAP/TAZ target sites lack these motifs.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis comparison between Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Nearly half of the YAP/TAZ target sites in MDA-MB-231 cells lack AP-1, TEAD, and STAT3 motifs.
source: The percentage of YAP/TAZ binding sites associated with AP-1, TEAD, and STAT3 motifs are comparable in both cell lines (compare Figure 6A with Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B), and nearly half of the YAP/TAZ target sites lack these motifs.
evidence: Supported by motif analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: TAZ-specific sites in MDA-MB-231 cells are enriched for ELF/ETS-family motifs.
source: As in ER-Src cells, TAZ-specific sites in MDA-MB-231 cells are enriched for ELF/ETS-family motifs (Figure 6—figure supplement 3E).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3E.

claim: The enrichment of CEBP motifs at YAP/TAZ target sites in ER-Src cells is not observed in MDA-MB-231 cells.
source: Interestingly, there are differences between the two cell lines with respect to how YAP/TAZ is recruited to some target loci. At YAP/TAZ target sites, the enrichment of CEBP motifs in ER-Src cells is not observed in MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment comparison between cell lines shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A,B.

claim: Motifs recognized by the RUNX tumor suppressor are significantly enriched in MDA-MB-231 cells but not in ER-Src cells.
source: Conversely, motifs recognized by the RUNX tumor suppressor are significantly enriched MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B), but not in ER-Src cells.
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Many genes associated with an individual motif are not associated with the other motifs.
source: Interestingly, many genes associated with an individual motif are not associated with the other motifs (Figure 6G).
evidence: Supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6G.

claim: YAP/TAZ sites differ in their GO enrichment terms based on the presumed recruiting motif.
source: In addition, YAP/TAZ sites differ in their GO enrichment terms based on the presumed recruiting motif (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: YAP/TAZ sites with an AP-1 motif are enriched for genes involved in morphogenesis and cell migration.
source: YAP/TAZ sites with an AP-1 motif are enriched for genes involved in morphogenesis and cell migration, whereas sites with a TEAD motif are enriched in genes involved in actin cytoskeletal organization.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: YAP/TAZ sites with a TEAD motif are enriched in genes involved in actin cytoskeletal organization.
source: YAP/TAZ sites with an AP-1 motif are enriched for genes involved in morphogenesis and cell migration, whereas sites with a TEAD motif are enriched in genes involved in actin cytoskeletal organization.
evidence: Supported by GO analysis shown in Supplementary file 4.

claim: RNA-seq analysis identifies between 1000 and 4000 differentially expressed genes for each factor when compared with a control siRNA.
source: RNA-seq analysis identifies between 1000 and 4000 differentially expressed genes for each condition when compared with a control siRNA.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis described in the Results section.

claim: Roughly equal numbers of genes show increased or decreased expression upon depletion of YAP, TAZ, JUNB, STAT3, or TEAD.
source: Roughly equal number of genes show increased or decreased expression with the directionality of differential expression nearly always preserved among factors (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: There is significant overlap between the differentially expressed genes identified upon deletion of each individual factor.
source: In accordance with previous results (Ji et al., 2018), there is significant overlap between the differentially expressed genes identified upon deletion of each individual factor (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by heatmap analysis shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Binding of YAP, TAZ, JUNB, STAT3, and TEAD is significantly more frequent at promoters of differentially expressed genes than at randomly generated control sets of protein-coding genes.
source: Notably, binding of these transcription factors is significantly more frequent at promoters of these differentially expressed genes than at randomly generated control sets of protein-coding genes (Figure 7C; p-value<0.01 for all factors).
evidence: Supported by binding frequency analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: High expression of the gene subset with YAP/TAZ sites having only AP-1 motifs is associated with significantly shorter survival in TNBC patients.
source: Notably, high expression of the gene subset with YAP/TAZ sites having only AP-1 motifs is associated with significantly shorter survival in TNBC patients (Figure 7D; p=0.023).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7D.

claim: High expression of the subset of genes containing YAP/TAZ sites with both AP-1 and TEAD motifs is significantly associated with shorter survival of TNBC patients.
source: Interestingly, high expression of the subset of genes containing YAP/TAZ sites with both AP-1 and TEAD motifs is even more significantly associated with shorter survival of TNBC patients (Figure 7F; p=0.002).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Survival is similar for patients with high or low expression of the full 1507 YAP/TAZ target genes.
source: In contrast, survival is similar for patients with high or low expression of the full 1507 YAP/TAZ target genes (Figure 7G; p-value=0.25).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7G.

claim: None of the gene sets examined are associated with significantly shorter survival in patients with the HER2+, luminal A, or luminal B forms of breast cancer.
source: None of the gene sets examined are associated with significantly shorter survival in patients with the HER2+, luminal A, or luminal B forms of breast cancer (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–D).
evidence: Supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: The Hippo pathway is active in ER-Src cells prior to transformation and is not altered during the transformation process.
source: This indicates that the Hippo pathway is active in this cell line prior to transformation and is not altered during the transformation process.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that YAP and TAZ protein levels in the nucleus are unchanged upon tamoxifen treatment.

claim: Differential crosslinking efficiencies of transcription factors at common target sites is distinct from monolithic complexes.
source: Such differential crosslinking efficiencies of transcription factors at common target sites is distinct from monolithic complexes (e.g., the Pol II preinitiation complex) where the crosslinking ratios among factors are invariant across all target sites (Kuras et al., 2000; Pokholok et al., 2002; Rhee and Pugh, 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In addition to TEAD proteins, AP-1 proteins and STAT3 can directly recruit YAP/TAZ to genomic sites.
source: Taken together with the direct protein–protein interactions, these results strongly suggest that, in addition to TEADs, AP-1 proteins and (to a lesser extent) STAT3 can directly recruit YAP/TAZ to genomic sites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from multiple lines of evidence including co-IP, ChIP-seq, motif analysis, and differential crosslinking.

claim: A complex of TEAD, JUNB, and STAT3 recruits YAP/TAZ to most target sites.
source: We provide evidence that a complex of TEAD, JUNB, and STAT3 recruits YAP/TAZ to most target sites, but that primary recruitment can be mediated by any one of these three proteins bound to their cognate motif.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the co-localization data, motif analysis, and differential crosslinking efficiencies.

claim: Primary recruitment of YAP/TAZ can be mediated by any one of TEAD, JUNB, or STAT3 bound to their cognate motif.
source: We provide evidence that a complex of TEAD, JUNB, and STAT3 recruits YAP/TAZ to most target sites, but that primary recruitment can be mediated by any one of these three proteins bound to their cognate motif.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the presence of individual motifs at YAP/TAZ target sites and differential crosslinking efficiencies.

claim: YAP and TAZ are important for STAT3 and AP-1 activity during breast epithelial cell transformation.
source: YAP and TAZ are important for STAT3 and AP-1 activity during breast epithelial cell transformation
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: YAP and TAZ have highly similar, but not identical, genomic binding profiles.
source: YAP and TAZ have highly similar, but not identical, genomic binding profiles
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by ChIP-seq data in Figure 4.

claim: YAP- and TAZ-specific sites differ in their associated motifs and biological functions from shared YAP/TAZ sites.
source: YAP- and TAZ-specific sites differ in their associated motifs and biological functions from shared YAP/TAZ sites
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by motif and GO analysis in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: YAP and TAZ co-occupy genomic target sites with STAT3, JUNB, and TEAD.
source: YAP and TAZ co-occupy genomic target sites with STAT3, JUNB, and TEAD
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by ChIP-seq and sequential ChIP data in Figure 5.

claim: YAP and TAZ can be recruited via AP-1, TEAD, and, to a lesser extent, STAT3 motifs.
source: YAP and TAZ can be recruited via AP-1, TEAD, and, to a lesser extent, STAT3 motifs
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by motif analysis in Figure 6.

claim: Different classes of YAP/TAZ target sites exist as defined by the recruiting motifs and protein crosslinking efficiencies.
source: Different classes of YAP/TAZ target sites as defined by the recruiting motifs and protein crosslinking efficiencies
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by motif analysis and crosslinking data in Figure 6.

claim: CEBP motifs are enriched at YAP/TAZ target sites.
source: CEBP motifs are enriched at YAP/TAZ target sites, and TAZ-specific sites are enriched for ETS motifs and depleted for AP-1 motifs
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by motif enrichment analysis in Figure 6.

claim: YAP and TAZ co-occupy sites with JUNB and STAT3 in a triple-negative breast cancer cell line.
source: YAP and TAZ co-occupy sites with JUNB and STAT3 in a triple-negative breast cancer cell line
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by ChIP-seq data in MDA-MB-231 cells shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Different classes of YAP/TAZ sites are associated with different categories of genes.
source: Different classes of YAP/TAZ sites are associated with different categories of genes
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by gene overlap and GO analysis in Figure 6G and Supplementary file 4.

claim: A common set of genes is regulated by YAP, TAZ, STAT3, JUNB, and TEAD.
source: A common set of genes regulated by YAP, TAZ, STAT3, JUNB, and TEAD
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by RNA-seq analysis in Figure 7A-B.

claim: AP-1 and TEAD classes of YAP/TAZ target genes are associated with poor prognosis in triple-negative breast cancers.
source: AP-1 and TEAD classes of YAP/TAZ target genes are associated with poor prognosis in triple-negative breast cancers
evidence: This is stated as a section heading and supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis in Figure 7D-F.
